title: Transdiagnostic efficacy of cognitive restructuring in adult populations from a gender perspective: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Background: Psychological science has developed a higher sensitivity towards inclusion and diversity. In this regard, researchers have analysed the effects that certain social categories, such as gender, can have on clinical and health psychology. Maladaptive cognitions can be affected by gender-related differences and their intersection with sociocultural aspects, especially when considering transgender and gender non-conforming people. Cognitive restructuring (CR) is a frequently employed technique for reframing cognitive schemas. However, it is also possible that it may be susceptible to influences linked to gender diversity factors. With the review projected in this protocol, we aim to evaluate the effectiveness of CR in reducing the severity of psychological symptoms, taking gender-related differences into account. Method: Systematic review. Databases will include PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science CORE, and Google Scholar for grey literature. Data will be screened by two reviewers and discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or a third reviewer if necessary. Extracted data will include general information, methodological data, and sample general and clinical characteristics. Conclusions: The forthcoming results will explore the role of gender identity in different outcomes following CR interventions, examining its contributions to provide more tailored and effective interventions.

title: Study planning is better served by Monte Carlo simulation than AI-generated participants
description: 'Silicon samples' – synthetic data generated by large language models prompted with demographic profiles – have been proposed as a useful method for planning human subjects research by providing useful effect size estimates. Monte Carlo simulation addresses the same planning problem from the opposite direction: the researcher specifies a data-generating process, then asks what follows. Monte Carlo simulation thus allow assumptions made about data-generating processes to be transparent and inspectable. Silicon samples by contrast bury these assumptions. In this article, I argue that this inscrutability, and consequences arising from it, makes silicon samples unsuitable for motivating study planning through effect size estimation. I conclude that researchers remain best-off sticking to Monte Carlo simulation for these purposes.

title: Conscious Awareness of the Decision to Stop is Distinct from the Perception of the Stop Signal
description: Although we constantly make and inhibit movements, it remains unresolved if we are consciously aware of the underlying decisions. Such investigations are confounded by the possibility that self-reports of these decisions may be retrospectively inferred from the movement. Instead, questions regarding conscious awareness may be better addressed during response inhibition where there is no overt movement. Here, using the anticipatory response inhibition task, we tested if participants could report the time when they decided to stop, and if it was distinct from the time when they perceived the stop signal. In study 1, following stop trials, participants reported when they decided to stop. The reported decision time preceded stop signal reaction time (SSRT), an estimate of the time taken to stop, by ~93ms and was positively correlated with SSRT. This suggested that participants could reliably report this decision. In study 2, participants reported when they perceived the stop signal. Perception time preceded SSRT by ~163ms and was positively correlated with SSRT. Thus, despite no difference in SSRT, the difference between perception time and decision time from SSRT were distinct suggesting that the two timings are separable mental events. In study 3, participants either reported the decision time or perception time. We replicated that the two timings were distinct despite no difference in SSRT - perception time and decision time preceded SSRT by ~138ms and ~57ms, respectively. This suggests that the decision to stop is a consciously accessible mental event which is distinct from the perception of the stop signal.

title: Transcranial Pulse Stimulation (TPS) as a Treatment for Cognitive Disorders in Aging: A Protocol for a Systematic Review
description: In an aging population with limited standard pharmacological treatment methods for cognitive disorders, the importance of non-invasive brain stimulation techniques – particularly Transcranial Pulse Stimulation (TPS) – is ever increasing. Though research on TPS in the treatment of cognitive disorders is present, there are currently no systematic reviews that focus solely on the use of TPS in cognitive disorders of aging. The primary objective of this literature review is to determine what cognitive disorders of aging have been studied with TPS as a treatment, and to narratively summarize what is known about the effectiveness of TPS treatment on neurocognitive performance and neuroimaging metrics. The study protocol will follow PRISMA-P guidelines and the completed review will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase and Scopus will be searched to find peer-reviewed primary literature. Included literature will focus on the use of TPS in the treatment of at least one cognitive disorder of aging, with the relevant population defined as adults 50 years old or older. Searching and screening will be organized in Covidence and both screening and data extraction will be completed by at least two independent reviewers. Data will be synthesized narratively, with a focus on general themes and patterns, accounting for expected heterogeneity. Primary outcomes will include cognitive disorder treated (e.g. Alzheimer’s disease, dementia, Mild Cognitive Impairment, etc.), treatment protocol (number of sessions, length of treatment, etc.), outcome measures split into cognitive performance measures and neuroimaging measures, reported side effects/adverse events and relevant results. Any additionally relevant outcomes will be considered as part of narrative completeness. No ethics approval is needed, and findings will be published in a peer-reviewed journal(s). This protocol is registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251246424).

title: Outgroup Representation in Close Networks Shows a Nonlinear Association With Mental Well-Being
description: Building on research linking social diversity to well-being, we examined how racial outgroup representation in individuals’ close social networks relates to mental well-being during two periods of heightened societal stress: the COVID-19 pandemic and a polarized election period. Across two large, nationally representative datasets (N = 4,955), we observed a curvilinear relationship: moderate racial outgroup representation was linked to the lowest levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, whereas both low and high outgroup representation were associated with worse outcomes. These associations were observed even after accounting for ingroup representation, outgroup dispersion, network size, and key demographic covariates. We then examined maladaptive and adaptive coping strategies and perceived social cohesion as candidate pathways. Moderate outgroup representation was consistently associated with lower maladaptive coping, whereas associations with adaptive coping were weaker and inconsistent. Data were consistent with an indirect linear effect of outgroup representation on well-being through increased perceived social cohesion, suggesting that although perceived social cohesion does not account for the observed curvilinear pattern, it is an important correlate of outgroup representation. Together, these findings emphasize that social network diversity has a nonlinear association with well-being and that targeting maladaptive coping may be particularly useful for promoting well-being in diverse contexts.
